To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stimulus-re-inforcer correlation in a response-independent discrete-trials, IRT>6 sec, procedure affects the rate of pecking but not the percentage of reinforced responses.

the effects of response-dependent and response-independent pairings and non-pairings of the light with food in the discrete trials IRT>6 sec procedure vary as a function whether the light was presented on the key or not.
the stimulus-re-inforcer correlation affects responding when the correlation is positive, but the effects vary as a function whether reinforcement is response-independent or response-dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the intertrial interval (ITI) on behavior in discrete trials procedures.
the effects of the rate of reinforcement in the intertrial intervals on the rate of pecking and the percentage of trials on which pecking is reinforced under the discrete-trials, IRT>t procedure.
the effects of stimulus-reinforcer correlations on the acquisition of operant behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of a stimulus-reinforcer contingency are a complex function of the nature and history of the contingency and the nature and history and the nature and intensity of the stimuli involved in the contingency.

the stimulus-reinerfor correlation affects responding, but that the nature of the effects of the correlation depends on the nature of the reinforcement schedule and the presence of background stimuli.

the stimulus-re-inforcer correlation in the discrete-trial IRT>6 sec procedure affects responding, but the effects of that correlation are not as great as the effects in a continuous-trials procedure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of background stimuli on behavior in discrete-trials IRI>6-sec procedures are a function of the correlation between the background and the response-reinforcer contingency.
the effects of stimulus-reinforcer correlations are not always consistent and are best accounted for by the effects of the correlations on the background stimuli.
the stimulus-re-inforcer correlation in a procedure with response-independent reinforcement is not the only determinant of the rate of response in the presence of a stimulus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the discrete-trials, IRT>6 condition is not a pure measure of conditioned reinforcement.
the stimulus-reinfocer correlation affects responding in a discrete trials IRT>6 sec procedure.
it is not enough to just look at the correlation of the stimulus and the response.
